---
title: "The Locked Cabinet"
---

::: {.ao-story}
In the deepest chamber of the Crypt lie sealed relics: keys, tokens and samples bound by special agreements. The Beast pads in behind you, curious, and its nose is already at the nearest seal. The warden will not let you carry the relics out, and she will not let the Beast see them. She asks you to learn which relics are yours to open and which belong to someone else.
:::

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will keep keys, settings and sensitive data out of the agent's reach, and know what changes on a shared cluster.
- **Before you start:** [Grow the Carapace](rules-of-the-carapace.html). A **deny rule** is a setting that blocks the agent's file-reading tool from a path. A **secret** is any credential, such as a password or key.
- **Time:** about 15 minutes.
:::

An agent reads whatever you point it at, and a hosted one sends it away, so the time to decide what it may see is before the first session. Much research data is not sensitive. Some of it is, and then special agreements apply. Your own data agreement and your cluster's policy come first. This quest uses no real data and practises **habits**, so that the careful choice becomes automatic.

## Three ideas

1. **A prompt may leave your machine.** With a hosted model, anything the agent reads may be sent to the provider. A model running locally (on your own machine, for example through Ollama) keeps prompts on your machine, though web or tool calls it makes may not. Your agreement decides whether either is allowed for your data.
2. **Secrets stay out of content.** API keys, tokens, SSH keys and passwords belong in a secret store, kept out of the project folder, and out of chats and any instructions file you commit. An environment variable (a named value the shell passes to every program it starts) is visible to any command the agent runs, so a read rule alone does not seal it.
3. **A shared cluster is shared.** What is fine on your laptop can disturb other people on a login node, or break a data policy on shared storage. Cluster rules apply to agents exactly as they apply to you.

::: {.callout-note}
A deny rule on your secrets files stops the agent's file-reading tool. It does not apply to a Python or Node script that opens the file itself. So also keep secrets out of the project folder, and use a sandbox or shell rules where you can. For another tool, check its documentation on shell reads of denied files.
:::

## Personal data and where an agent may send it

- **Reading a file discloses it.** With an externally hosted model, everything the agent reads goes to the provider. If the agent opens a project `.env` file, treat its keys as exposed and rotate them (replace them with new ones). Keep secrets outside folders the agent can read.
- **Personal data needs more than a no-training promise.** Sending personal data to a provider can count as processing under GDPR (the EU data protection law). Ask your data steward which accounts are approved, and use an institutional account for work. Ask them too whether you need a lawful basis (a legal reason to process), a processor contract (a written agreement with the provider) and a transfer basis (a legal route for sending data abroad).
- **Limit where the agent can send data.** Instructions alone do not stop a send. A sandbox or network limit can.

## What stays behind: transcripts

The agent keeps a record of the session so that it can resume. Anything that passes through a tool goes into that record: file contents, command output, pasted text. If a tool reads a `.env` file or a command prints a credential, the value is written to the session transcript. Transcripts are stored locally in plaintext, for 30 days by default.

In late 2026 a coding-tool vendor reported an incident (first announced on 29 October, with details in an update dated 13 November): an access key issued to one of its vendors was exposed, and a storage bucket held limited coding agent traces. A small number of those traces contained credentials that had not been redacted.

Habits that cost little:

1. **Reference a secret, do not type it.** Write `psql "$DATABASE_URL"`, so the command, and any rule saved from it, holds a variable's name.
2. **Approve patterns, not literal commands** (`npm run *`). When you choose "Yes, and don't ask again", Claude Code saves an `allow` rule in `.claude/settings.local.json`. On first write in a git repository it adds that file to your global git excludes. If you create the file by hand, add it to `.gitignore` yourself. Open the file now and then, and delete any saved rule that contains a secret.
3. **Rotate anything that has been in a transcript** (replace it with a new key and disable the old one). Deleting the file does not reach backups, copies or a vendor's storage.
4. **Keep less.** The `cleanupPeriodDays` setting shortens how long transcripts stay. `claude purge` deletes a project's state (try `--dry-run` first). `CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY=1` skips writing transcripts and prompt history.
5. **Make a leak worth little.** A token for one repository that expires in an hour is a small loss if it leaks. A GitHub installation access token expires after 1 hour. Where a service only issues long-lived keys, give the agent a separate, narrow key that you can rotate without breaking your own work.

On the OpenCode route the same habits apply with different names. Choosing **Allow always** saves the proposed patterns as allow rules for the project, so open that config now and then too. OpenCode keeps its sessions in a local database in its data folder (`opencode debug paths` prints the folder). `opencode session list` shows the sessions and `opencode session delete` removes one. Anything an agent read can sit in that database, so rotate a secret that appeared in a session.

Redaction helps and has limits. A scanner matches formats, and a password after `-p` has none.

## Unpublished ideas and results

A common worry: *my unpublished results or ideas will leak and someone will get there first.* The habits below lower the chance and the cost of being wrong.

Training use means a provider may learn from your prompts to improve future models. For Claude Code:

- For Free, Pro, Max and Ultra accounts, training use depends on a privacy setting that you can change.
- For Team, Enterprise and API accounts, code and prompts sent to Claude Code are not used for training under commercial terms, unless the customer opts in.
- Retention for consumer accounts is 5 years if you allow model improvement and 30 days if you do not. Commercial accounts have 30 days as standard, and zero data retention for qualified Enterprise accounts.
- Read the terms of the exact tool and plan you use, including the privacy page of any chat app. Other providers' terms differ by product and plan; read the terms for the exact plan you use.

Habits:

1. **Keep unpublished ideas, results and sequences out of consumer chat tools** unless the terms say how your text is used and you accept that.
2. **Prefer an agreement your institution has reviewed.** Ask your data steward or research office what is approved. They can advise on contracts and ownership.
3. **Consider a local model.** Ollama does not see your prompts or data when you run locally. Tools and web calls the model makes may still send data out. A free hosted tier still sends your prompts to a provider.
4. **Date-stamp your work.** A preprint, a repository tag or a dated lab notebook entry records when you had it.
5. **Share on a need-to-know basis.** Send collaborators what they need for the task.

## Bonus

Nothing here is checked, and nothing depends on it. The real rules are in a document your group holds.

<div data-ao-honour="find-agreement" data-xp="20">Find the data-handling agreement or policy that applies to your project (or ask your group leader where it is). Read the passages about <strong>where data may be processed</strong> and <strong>whether it may be sent to external services</strong>, and write down in your own notes what they say.</div>

<div data-ao-honour="find-secrets" data-xp="10">List where your own API keys and settings files live (for example a <code>.env</code> file or a shell profile), and check that your agent's permission rules deny reading them.</div>

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Data usage](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/data-usage): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what is sent to the provider, how training and retention differ by plan, and what telemetry can be turned off. It does not replace your own data agreement.
- [Security](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/security): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it covers prompt injection, credential storage and advice for sensitive code.
- [AI for Science, practice 11: decide where research data may go](https://aiforscience.eu/best-practices/11-decide-where-research-data-may-go/): AI for Science (European draft best practices), docs. Why read: it ties the choice of service to the contract and legal basis for your data, and limits agent sends through the environment. A draft with no endorsements yet; it is not legal advice.
- [Configure permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows the deny rules that keep the agent's file tools away from files such as `.env`.
- [The .claude directory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it says what is written to transcripts on disk, how long it stays, and how `claude purge` clears it.
- [Settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it explains where "don't ask again" approvals are saved and how `settings.local.json` is kept out of git.
- [An update on our recent security incident](https://cursor.com/blog/security-incident-update): Cursor, article. Why read: a first-hand account of agent traces with unredacted credentials.
- [Authenticating as a GitHub App installation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/authenticating-as-a-github-app-installation): GitHub, docs. Why read: it shows the one-hour token that keeps a leak small.
:::
